questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the colour change of litmus when an acid is added to it?

key_points: Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — Blue litmus turns red. Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue.

questions.text: Name two natural substances that can be used as acid-base indicators. State the colour change each shows in acidic and basic solutions.

key_points: Any two: turmeric (yellow in acid, red in base); red cabbage (red in acid, green/yellow in base); litmus (red in acid, blue in base)
Both colour changes stated
rubric.expected_answer: Two natural indicators: (1) Turmeric — yellow in acidic solution, red/pink in basic solution. (2) Red cabbage juice — red/pink in acid, green/yellow in base. (Also acceptable: litmus — red in acid, blue in base.)

questions.text: What happens when zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid?

options.text: ZnSO4 and H2 gas are produced

key_points: Metals + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen gas
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — ZnSO4 and H2 gas are produced. When a metal reacts with a dilute acid: metal + acid produces salt + hydrogen gas. Zn + H2SO4 produces ZnSO4 + H2.

questions.text: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to ammonium sulphate solution and the mixture is heated. The gas evolved turns moist red litmus paper blue. The gas is:

key_points: Base reacts with ammonium salt to release NH3; NH3 is basic
rubric.expected_answer: Option A — Ammonia (NH3). A base (NaOH) reacts with an ammonium salt to release NH3 gas. NH3 is basic and turns moist red litmus blue.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic property of acids?

options.text: They produce H+ ions in aqueous solution
They react with metals to liberate hydrogen
They feel soapy and slippery to touch

key_points: Soapy/slippery feel is a property of bases, not acids
rubric.expected_answer: Option D — "They feel soapy and slippery to touch" is NOT a property of acids; it is a property of bases/alkalis. Acids are corrosive and sour, not soapy.

questions.text: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution. Name the type of this reaction.

key_points: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O
Neutralisation reaction
rubric.expected_answer: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l); Neutralisation reaction

questions.text: A student adds dilute hydrochloric acid to sodium carbonate. (a) Write the balanced equation for the reaction. (b) What is the observation?

key_points: Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2
Brisk effervescence of CO2 gas; gas turns lime water milky
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Na2CO3 + 2HCl produces 2NaCl + H2O + CO2. (b) Observation: brisk effervescence (bubbling) of CO2 gas; the gas turns lime water milky.

questions.text: Explain why dry HCl gas does not turn blue litmus red, but HCl dissolved in water does. What does this tell us about the nature of HCl?

key_points: Dry HCl has no water → cannot ionise → no H+ ions → no acidic properties
HCl in water: HCl → H+ + Cl- ; H+ (or H3O+) responsible for acidity
Shows water is required for ionisation; HCl itself is a covalent compound
rubric.expected_answer: Dry HCl is a covalent compound and does not dissociate without water. When dissolved in water it produces H+ (H3O+) ions which cause acidic properties like turning litmus red.

questions.text: 10 mL of NaOH solution is exactly neutralised by 8 mL of a given HCl solution. How many mL of the same HCl solution will be required to neutralise 20 mL of the same NaOH solution?

key_points: Use proportion: V_HCl / V_NaOH = constant
rubric.expected_answer: 16 mL

questions.text: What are the chemical properties of acids? Describe with balanced equations: (a) reaction with a metal, (b) reaction with a metal oxide, (c) reaction with a metal carbonate. Give one example each.

key_points: (a) Metal + acid → salt + H2 e.g. Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2
(b) Metal oxide + acid → salt + water e.g. CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O (base-acid = neutralisation)
(c) Metal carbonate + acid → salt + water + CO2 e.g. Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2
All three equations balanced; one example each
rubric.expected_answer: Chemical properties of acids: (a) Metal + acid produces salt + H2: Zn + H2SO4 produces ZnSO4 + H2. (b) Metal oxide + acid produces salt + water (neutralisation): CuO + H2SO4 produces CuSO4 + H2O. (c) Metal carbonate + acid produces salt + water + CO2: Na2CO3 + 2HCl produces 2NaCl + H2O + CO2.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): When excess CO2 is passed into lime water, the milky white precipitate dissolves and the solution becomes clear.
Reason (R): Calcium carbonate formed in the first step reacts with excess CO2 and water to form soluble calcium bicarbonate.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

key_points: CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O → Ca(HCO3)2 (soluble); both A and R correct
rubric.expected_answer: Option A — Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Excess CO2 reacts with CaCO3 and water to form soluble Ca(HCO3)2, dissolving the white precipitate: CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O produces Ca(HCO3)2.

questions.text: Draw a labelled diagram to show the laboratory test for hydrogen gas produced when a metal reacts with a dilute acid. Label: flask, acid + metal, delivery tube, gas collected, burning splint test.

key_points: Flask labelled with metal + acid
Delivery tube shown
Collection vessel / gas jar labelled
Test: burning splint shows pop sound
rubric.expected_answer: Diagram should show: a flask containing metal (e.g. Zn) + dilute acid (e.g. H2SO4), a delivery tube leading to a collection vessel for H2 gas, and a burning splint at the mouth of the tube showing a "pop" sound as the test for hydrogen.

questions.text: When hydrogen chloride gas is dissolved in water, what ions are produced?

key_points: HCl → H+ + Cl-  (or HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl-)
rubric.expected_answer: Option A — H+ (H3O+) and Cl-. HCl dissolved in water ionises: HCl + H2O produces H3O+ + Cl-. The hydronium ion H3O+ is responsible for acidic properties.

questions.text: What are Arrhenius definitions of acids and bases? Give one example of each.

key_points: Acid: substance that produces H+ ions in water (e.g. HCl, H2SO4)
Base: substance that produces OH- ions in water (e.g. NaOH, KOH)
rubric.expected_answer: Arrhenius acid: a substance that produces H+ ions in aqueous solution (e.g. HCl produces H+ + Cl-). Arrhenius base: a substance that produces OH- ions in aqueous solution (e.g. NaOH produces Na+ + OH-).

questions.text: Distinguish between a strong acid and a weak acid. Give one example of each. How do their degrees of ionisation differ?

key_points: Strong acid: completely ionises in water (e.g. HCl, H2SO4)
Weak acid: partially ionises in water (e.g. acetic acid, carbonic acid)
Strong acid: degree of ionisation ≈ 1 (100%); weak acid << 1
rubric.expected_answer: Strong acid: completely ionises in water — degree of ionisation ~100% (e.g. HCl, H2SO4). Weak acid: partially ionises in water — degree of ionisation much less than 100% (e.g. acetic acid CH3COOH, carbonic acid H2CO3). Strong acids have much higher H+ concentration than weak acids at the same molarity.

questions.text: Why do solutions of acids and bases conduct electricity? What type of particles are responsible?

key_points: Acids and bases ionise in water to produce ions
Ions (H+, OH-, anions, cations) are mobile charged particles
Mobile ions carry electric charge through the solution
rubric.expected_answer: Acids and bases are electrolytes. In water they dissociate into ions (e.g. H+ and Cl-). These mobile ions carry electric charge and thus the solution conducts electricity.

questions.text: A sample of 12 mL of HCl solution exactly neutralises 15 mL of NaOH solution. What volume of the same HCl solution will be needed to neutralise 25 mL of the same NaOH solution? (Show your working.)

key_points: V_HCl / V_NaOH = 12/15 = 4/5
rubric.expected_answer: 20 mL

questions.text:
Assertion (A): All acidic solutions conduct electricity.
Reason (R): All acids produce H+ ions in water and these ions carry electric current.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

key_points: Acids ionise to give H+ (and anion); ions conduct electricity; both A and R correct
rubric.expected_answer: Option A — Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Acids ionise in water to give H+ ions (and anions); these mobile ions carry electric charge, allowing conduction.

questions.text: The pH of a solution is 3. The solution is:

key_points: pH < 7 → acidic; pH 3 is strongly acidic
rubric.expected_answer: Option A — Strongly acidic. pH 3 is well below 7, indicating a high H+ concentration. pH scale: 0-7 is acidic; closer to 0 means more strongly acidic.

questions.text: A solution has a pH of 11. What will happen if you add a small amount of acid to it?

key_points: Adding acid increases H+; OH- concentration decreases; pH moves towards neutral
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — pH decreases towards 7. Adding acid increases H+ concentration, which neutralises some OH- ions, reducing the pH from 11 toward neutral (7), but not instantly to 7 unless exactly stoichiometric.

questions.text: What is the pH scale? State the pH of (a) a neutral solution, (b) a strong acid, (c) a strong base.

key_points: pH scale: 0–14; measures H+ concentration in a solution
(a) Neutral: pH 7  (b) Strong acid: pH < 7 (e.g. 1–2)  (c) Strong base: pH > 7 (e.g. 13–14)
rubric.expected_answer: The pH scale measures acidity/alkalinity from 0 to 14 based on H+ concentration. (a) Neutral solution: pH = 7. (b) Strong acid: pH < 7 (e.g., 1-2). (c) Strong base: pH > 7 (e.g., 13-14).

questions.text: How does the pH of the soil affect plant growth? What is the ideal pH range for most crops?

key_points: Most plants grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 6–7)
Very acidic or very basic soil affects nutrient availability and root function
Farmers add lime (CaO) to correct acidic soil
rubric.expected_answer: Most crops grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 6-7). Soil with very low or very high pH reduces nutrient availability and damages roots. Farmers add quicklime (CaO) or slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) to raise the pH of acidic soil.

questions.text: Why does the mouth become acidic after eating sugar-rich foods? How does toothpaste help? Relate your answer to pH.

key_points: Bacteria in mouth break down sugar to produce acids
pH in mouth drops below 5.5 → enamel corrodes (tooth decay)
Toothpaste is basic (alkaline); neutralises the acid; raises pH above 5.5
rubric.expected_answer: Bacteria in the mouth degrade sugars to produce acids. This lowers the pH of the mouth below 5.5, causing dissolution of enamel (tooth decay). Toothpastes are basic in nature; they neutralise the acid and raise the pH, preventing tooth decay.

questions.text: Describe the importance of pH in everyday life with reference to: (a) digestion in the human body, (b) self-defence in animals and plants, (c) acid rain and its effects.

key_points: (a) Stomach secretes HCl (pH 1.5–2); enzymes work in this acidic medium for protein digestion; antacids neutralise excess acid
(b) Bee sting: formic/methanoic acid (acidic); wasp sting: alkaline; plants like nettle have formic acid
(c) Acid rain: SO2 + NO2 dissolve in rainwater → H2SO4/HNO3; pH < 5.6; corrodes buildings (marble/limestone), harms aquatic life, damages crops
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Stomach secretes HCl (pH 1.5-2); enzymes like pepsin work in this acidic medium for protein digestion; antacids neutralise excess acid. (b) Bee sting: formic (methanoic) acid (acidic); wasp sting: alkaline; nettle plant contains formic acid. (c) Acid rain: SO2 + NO2 dissolve in rainwater forming H2SO4/HNO3; pH drops below 5.6, corroding marble buildings and harming aquatic life and crops.

questions.text: Draw a pH scale from 0 to 14. Mark on it: (a) pH of gastric juice, (b) pH of blood, (c) pH of lemon juice, (d) pH of a neutral solution, (e) pH of household bleach (NaOCl).

key_points: Scale drawn 0–14
Acidic region 0–7 labelled
Basic region 7–14 labelled
Five substances placed approximately correctly
rubric.expected_answer: Diagram: a horizontal scale from 0 to 14, marked "Acidic" (0-7) and "Basic/Alkaline" (7-14), neutral at 7. Approximate placements: (a) gastric juice ~pH 1-2, (b) blood ~pH 7.4, (c) lemon juice ~pH 2-3, (d) neutral solution pH 7, (e) bleach (NaOCl) ~pH 11-12.

questions.text: What type of salt is formed when a strong acid reacts with a weak base?

key_points: Strong acid + weak base → acidic salt; e.g. NH4Cl
rubric.expected_answer: Option A — Acidic salt (pH < 7). A strong acid + weak base produces a salt that hydrolyses in water to give H+ ions (acidic solution, pH < 7). Example: NH4Cl (from HCl + NH4OH).

questions.text: What is a salt? Give the formula of the salt formed between (a) H2SO4 and KOH, (b) HNO3 and Ca(OH)2.

key_points: Salt: ionic compound formed by neutralisation of acid by base
(a) H2SO4 + 2KOH → K2SO4 + 2H2O → K2SO4
(b) 2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 → Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O → Ca(NO3)2
rubric.expected_answer: A salt is an ionic compound formed by the neutralisation of an acid by a base. (a) H2SO4 + 2KOH produces K2SO4 + 2H2O; salt = potassium sulphate (K2SO4). (b) 2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 produces Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O; salt = calcium nitrate (Ca(NO3)2).

questions.text: What is the water of crystallisation? Name the compound that contains 10 water molecules of crystallisation. Write its formula and state one use.

key_points: Water of crystallisation: fixed number of water molecules chemically bonded in a crystalline salt
Washing soda: Na2CO3.10H2O; used as cleansing agent / water softener
rubric.expected_answer: Water of crystallisation is a fixed number of water molecules chemically bonded in the crystal structure of a salt. The compound with 10 water molecules is washing soda: Na2CO3.10H2O (sodium carbonate decahydrate). It is used as a cleansing agent and water softener.

questions.text: Explain why aqueous solution of common salt (NaCl) is neutral, whereas aqueous solution of sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) is basic.

key_points: NaCl: strong acid (HCl) + strong base (NaOH); ions do not hydrolyse water → neutral
Na2CO3: strong base (NaOH) + weak acid (H2CO3); CO3(2-) hydrolyses water to give OH- → basic
rubric.expected_answer: NaCl is formed from a strong acid (HCl) and a strong base (NaOH). Both ions are spectators and do not react with water, so the solution is neutral (pH 7). Na2CO3 is formed from NaOH (strong base) and H2CO3 (weak acid). The carbonate ion (CO3^2-) hydrolyses water to produce OH- ions, making the solution basic (pH > 7).

questions.text: What is the importance of pH in everyday life with special reference to salts? Explain: (a) how washing soda (Na2CO3) is prepared from baking soda, (b) the use of baking powder in cooking.

key_points: (a) NaHCO3 heated → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; Na2CO3 rehydrated → washing soda
(b) Baking powder = NaHCO3 + edible acid (e.g. tartaric acid); on heating/moisture, CO2 released → dough rises; tartaric acid neutralises Na2CO3 taste
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Washing soda from baking soda: 2NaHCO3 (heat) produces Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; rehydrate Na2CO3 to get Na2CO3.10H2O. (b) Baking powder = NaHCO3 + edible acid (tartaric acid); on heating or with moisture, CO2 is released making dough rise; tartaric acid also neutralises the Na2CO3 formed so food does not taste bitter.

questions.text: The process of electrolysis of brine produces which three important chemicals?

key_points: Chlor-alkali process: NaCl solution electrolysis → NaOH + Cl2 + H2
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — NaOH, Cl2, and H2. Electrolysis of brine (NaCl solution) in the chlor-alkali process produces sodium hydroxide (NaOH) at the cathode region, chlorine gas (Cl2) at the anode, and hydrogen gas (H2) at the cathode.

questions.text: State any two uses each of: (a) chlorine gas, (b) hydrogen gas, obtained from the chlor-alkali process.

key_points: Cl2: (1) manufacture of PVC/pesticides (2) disinfection of water / bleaching agents
H2: (1) manufacture of NH3 (Haber process) (2) hydrogenation of oils → margarine / HCl production
rubric.expected_answer: Chlorine gas (Cl2) uses: (1) manufacture of PVC, pesticides, and CFCs; (2) disinfecting drinking water and making bleaching agents. Hydrogen gas (H2) uses: (1) manufacture of ammonia (Haber process) and hydrochloric acid; (2) hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make margarine.

questions.text: Write the formula of bleaching powder and give two uses of bleaching powder.

key_points: Formula: Ca(OCl)Cl (calcium oxychloride)
Uses: (1) bleaching cotton/linen/washed clothes (2) disinfecting drinking water
rubric.expected_answer: Formula of bleaching powder: Ca(OCl)Cl (calcium oxychloride). Uses: (1) bleaching cotton, linen, and washed clothes in the textile industry; (2) disinfecting drinking water and swimming pools.

questions.text: Describe the chlor-alkali process. Draw a labelled diagram of the electrolytic cell. Write the electrode reactions and state the products obtained, and their uses.

key_points: Brine (NaCl solution) is electrolysed
Cathode: 2H+ + 2e- → H2 (reduction); H2 collected at cathode
Anode: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e- (oxidation); Cl2 collected at anode
NaOH formed in solution around cathode
Diagram with cell, electrodes, products labelled
Uses: H2 (fuel, margarine), Cl2 (bleach, PVC), NaOH (soap, detergent)
rubric.expected_answer: The chlor-alkali process electrolyses brine (NaCl solution). At the cathode: 2H+ + 2e- produces H2 (reduction). At the anode: 2Cl- produces Cl2 + 2e- (oxidation). NaOH forms in solution near the cathode. Overall: 2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) produces 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) + H2(g). Uses: H2 (fuel, making margarine), Cl2 (bleach, PVC), NaOH (soap, detergent manufacturing). Diagram should show electrolytic cell with labelled electrodes, gas outlets, and NaOH collection.

questions.text: Plaster of Paris is obtained by heating gypsum. What is the chemical formula of Plaster of Paris?

key_points: Gypsum: CaSO4.2H2O; heated at 373 K → CaSO4.1/2H2O (Plaster of Paris)
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — CaSO4.0.5H2O (Plaster of Paris). Gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O) heated at 373 K loses 1.5 molecules of water to form the hemihydrate CaSO4.1/2H2O, known as Plaster of Paris.

questions.text: 15 mL of H2SO4 solution exactly neutralises 30 mL of NaOH solution. How many mL of the same H2SO4 solution will be required to neutralise 12 mL of the same NaOH solution?

rubric.expected_answer: 6 mL

questions.text: Which indicator turns pink/red in acidic solution and colourless in basic solution?

key_points: Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in base
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — Phenolphthalein. It is colourless in acidic and neutral solutions, and turns pink/red in basic solutions. Note: the question states pink in acid, but phenolphthalein is actually colourless in acid and pink in base.

questions.text: Olfactory indicators are substances that:

options.text: Change their smell in acid or base
Smell the same regardless of pH
Produce a gas when added to acid

key_points: Olfactory indicators change their smell/odour in acidic vs basic medium
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — Olfactory indicators change their smell/odour in acidic or basic medium. Examples: onion loses its smell in basic solution; vanilla extract loses its characteristic smell in basic solution.

questions.text: How would you use red cabbage juice as an indicator? Describe what colour changes you would observe in an acid and in a base.

key_points: Extract red cabbage juice; add to test solutions
Acidic solution: red/pink colour; Basic solution: green/yellow colour
rubric.expected_answer: Boil red cabbage and collect the purple juice. Add a few drops to test solutions. In acidic solution the juice turns red/pink; in basic solution it turns green/yellow. The colour change is due to anthocyanin pigments that respond to pH changes.

questions.text: A metal carbonate reacts with an acid. What gases are produced in this reaction?

key_points: Metal carbonate + acid → salt + water + CO2
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — CO2 and H2O (steam). Metal carbonate + acid produces salt + water + CO2. Example: CaCO3 + 2HCl produces CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct equation for the reaction of CaO with water?

key_points: CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime); exothermic
rubric.expected_answer: Option A — CaO + H2O produces Ca(OH)2. This reaction is exothermic and produces slaked lime (calcium hydroxide). It is used to treat acidic soil.

questions.text: What happens when a small piece of sodium is dropped into water? Write the equation and identify the products.

key_points: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2↑
Products: sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and hydrogen gas (H2)
Reaction is vigorous/exothermic; H2 may catch fire
rubric.expected_answer: When sodium is dropped in water it reacts vigorously: 2Na + 2H2O produces 2NaOH + H2. Products are sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and hydrogen gas (H2). The reaction is highly exothermic; the heat may ignite the H2 gas, causing a flame.

questions.text: Explain with an equation how washing soda (Na2CO3) acts as a base.

key_points: Na2CO3 is a salt of a strong base and a weak acid
CO3(2-) + H2O ⇌ HCO3- + OH-; OH- makes solution basic
rubric.expected_answer: Washing soda (Na2CO3) is a salt of a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (H2CO3). When dissolved in water, the carbonate ion hydrolyses: CO3(2-) + H2O produces HCO3- + OH-. The OH- ions make the solution basic (pH > 7), so Na2CO3 acts as a base.

questions.text: An antacid tablet contains NaHCO3. How does it relieve indigestion? Write the chemical equation.

key_points: Stomach produces excess HCl causing indigestion
NaHCO3 + HCl → NaCl + H2O + CO2
NaHCO3 neutralises excess acid; CO2 released
rubric.expected_answer: NaHCO3 is basic. It neutralises excess HCl in the stomach: NaHCO3 + HCl → NaCl + H2O + CO2. This reduces acidity and relieves indigestion.

questions.text: If 25 mL of HCl solution neutralises 20 mL of NaOH solution, what volume of HCl is needed to neutralise 35 mL of the same NaOH solution?
When HCl gas is dissolved in toluene (a non-polar organic solvent), the solution does NOT conduct electricity. Why?

options.text: HCl gas is insoluble in toluene
HCl does not ionise in toluene as there is no water

key_points: No water → no ionisation → no ions → no conduction
rubric.expected_answer: Option D — HCl does not ionise in toluene as there is no water. Water is required for ionisation of HCl into H+ and Cl- ions; without ions, the solution cannot conduct electricity. Toluene is a non-polar solvent that does not facilitate ionisation.

questions.text: Define the term 'ionisation'. Why is water necessary for acids and bases to show their properties?

key_points: Ionisation: breaking of a compound into its constituent ions
Water provides medium for ionisation; H+ and OH- ions are only produced when dissolved in water
rubric.expected_answer: Ionisation is the process by which a compound dissociates (breaks apart) into its constituent ions in a solvent. Water is necessary because it provides a polar medium that stabilises ions by solvation (hydration). Without water, acids and bases remain as covalent compounds and do not produce H+ or OH- ions.

questions.text: What is the difference between an acid and a base in terms of ions they produce in water? Give two examples of each.

key_points: Acid: produces H+ (or H3O+) ions in water; e.g. HCl, H2SO4
Base: produces OH- ions in water; e.g. NaOH, KOH
rubric.expected_answer: Acids produce H+ ions (or H3O+ ions) in water; examples: HCl produces H+ + Cl-, H2SO4 produces 2H+ + SO4(2-). Bases produce OH- ions in water; examples: NaOH produces Na+ + OH-, KOH produces K+ + OH-.

questions.text: A student tested two solutions A and B with a conductivity apparatus. Solution A glowed brightly; solution B glowed dimly. What can you conclude about A and B? Relate to ionisation.

key_points: Bright glow → more ions → A is a strong electrolyte (e.g. strong acid/base; completely ionised)
Dim glow → fewer ions → B is a weak electrolyte (e.g. weak acid/base; partially ionised)
Relates to degree of ionisation
rubric.expected_answer: Brightness ∝ ion concentration. A glows brightly → high ion concentration → A is a strong electrolyte (completely ionised, e.g. HCl). B glows dimly → fewer ions → B is a weak electrolyte (partially ionised, e.g. CH3COOH).

questions.text: What is the pH of pure water at 25°C?

key_points: Pure water: [H+] = [OH-]; pH = 7
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — pH 7. Pure water at 25 degrees C has equal concentrations of H+ and OH- ions ([H+] = [OH-] = 10^-7 M), making it perfectly neutral at pH 7.

questions.text: Acid rain has a pH less than:

key_points: Normal rain: pH ~5.6 (dissolved CO2); pH < 5.6 → acid rain
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — 5.6. Normal rain dissolves atmospheric CO2 forming weak carbonic acid, giving a natural pH of ~5.6. When SO2 and NO2 dissolve in rainwater, pH drops below 5.6, making it acid rain.

questions.text: How is pH of blood maintained in our body? What happens if pH of blood goes outside the normal range?

key_points: Blood pH maintained between 7.35–7.45 by buffer systems
Outside this range: enzymes stop working; acidosis (pH < 7.35) or alkalosis (pH > 7.45) → fatal
rubric.expected_answer: Blood pH is maintained between 7.35-7.45 by buffer systems (e.g. carbonate-bicarbonate buffer). If pH falls below 7.35 (acidosis) or rises above 7.45 (alkalosis), enzymes stop functioning, metabolism is disrupted, and the condition becomes life-threatening.

questions.text: A farmer's soil has pH 4. What should the farmer do to make it suitable for growing most crops? Explain the chemistry.

key_points: pH 4 = strongly acidic; most crops need pH 6–7
Add quicklime (CaO) or slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) or chalk (CaCO3)
Basic substance neutralises excess acid, raising pH
rubric.expected_answer: The farmer should add quicklime (CaO), slaked lime (Ca(OH)2), or chalk (CaCO3) to the acidic soil. These basic substances neutralise the excess acid, raising the pH to the ideal range of 6-7 for most crops. Example: Ca(OH)2 + H2SO4 produces CaSO4 + 2H2O.

questions.text: Name two acids present in the human body and state where they are found and what role they play.

key_points: HCl: in stomach (gastric juice); pH 1.5–2; activates pepsin for protein digestion
Lactic acid: produced in muscles during anaerobic respiration; causes muscle fatigue/soreness
(Also accept: amino acids in proteins, nucleic acids in DNA/RNA)
rubric.expected_answer: Two acids in the human body: (1) Hydrochloric acid (HCl) — found in gastric juice (stomach); activates pepsin and kills bacteria during digestion. (2) Lactic acid — produced in muscles during anaerobic respiration (vigorous exercise); causes muscle fatigue and soreness.

questions.text: A solution has [H+] concentration 10 times higher than pure water. What is its pH? Is it acidic or basic? (Note: pH of pure water = 7.)

key_points: Pure water [H+] = 10^-7 M; 10x higher = 10^-6 M
pH 6 < 7 → acidic
rubric.expected_answer: pH = 6; acidic

questions.text: Gypsum has the formula CaSO4.2H2O. On strong heating, it loses water to form:

key_points: Gypsum heated at 373 K → Plaster of Paris (CaSO4.½H2O)
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — CaSO4.0.5H2O (Plaster of Paris). Gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O) loses 1.5 molecules of water when heated at 373 K, forming CaSO4.1/2H2O.

questions.text: What is the common name and formula of (a) baking soda, (b) washing soda, (c) bleaching powder?

key_points: (a) Baking soda: NaHCO3 (sodium hydrogen carbonate)
(b) Washing soda: Na2CO3.10H2O (sodium carbonate decahydrate)
(c) Bleaching powder: Ca(OCl)Cl (calcium oxychloride)
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Baking soda: NaHCO3 (sodium hydrogen carbonate / sodium bicarbonate). (b) Washing soda: Na2CO3.10H2O (sodium carbonate decahydrate). (c) Bleaching powder: Ca(OCl)Cl (calcium oxychloride).

questions.text: Plaster of Paris sets when mixed with water. Explain why with a chemical equation.

key_points: CaSO4.½H2O + 1½H2O → CaSO4.2H2O (gypsum)
Takes up water of crystallisation → forms interlocking crystals → hard solid
rubric.expected_answer: Plaster of Paris (CaSO4.1/2H2O) sets when mixed with water because it rehydrates to form gypsum: CaSO4.1/2H2O + 1.5H2O produces CaSO4.2H2O. The gypsum crystals interlock as they form, creating a hard rigid solid.

questions.text: How would you test whether a given salt is acidic, basic or neutral without a pH meter? Describe two methods.

key_points: Method 1: dissolve in water, test with litmus paper; red→acidic, blue→basic, no change→neutral
Method 2: use universal indicator/pH paper; match colour to pH chart
(Also: phenolphthalein: colourless in acid/neutral, pink in base)
rubric.expected_answer: Method 1: Dissolve the salt in water and test with litmus paper — red litmus turns blue (basic); blue litmus turns red (acidic); no change (neutral). Method 2: Use universal indicator paper or pH paper; compare the colour to the pH chart. (Also: phenolphthalein is colourless in acid/neutral and pink in base.)

questions.text: 5 mL of an acid solution neutralises 10 mL of a base solution. What volume of acid is needed to neutralise 15 mL of the same base?

rubric.expected_answer: 7.5 mL

questions.text: Baking soda is used in fire extinguishers because on heating it produces:

key_points: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; CO2 is non-combustible, smothers fire
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — CO2 gas. When NaHCO3 (baking soda) is heated: 2NaHCO3 produces Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. CO2 is non-combustible and denser than air, smothering the fire by cutting off its oxygen supply.

questions.text: What is the full name of NaOH? State three industrial uses of sodium hydroxide.

key_points: NaOH = Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda)
Uses: (1) soap/detergent manufacture (2) paper industry (3) textile / de-greasing metals
rubric.expected_answer: Full name of NaOH: Sodium hydroxide (also called caustic soda). Industrial uses: (1) manufacture of soap and detergents; (2) paper and pulp industry; (3) manufacture of textiles (rayon) and de-greasing metals.

questions.text: Why is Plaster of Paris stored in moisture-proof containers? What happens if it absorbs moisture?

key_points: Plaster of Paris (CaSO4.½H2O) reacts with water to form gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O)
If it absorbs moisture it will set/harden and become unusable
rubric.expected_answer: Plaster of Paris must be stored in moisture-proof containers because it readily reacts with water: CaSO4.1/2H2O + 1.5H2O produces CaSO4.2H2O (gypsum). If it absorbs moisture from the air, it will harden and set, making it unusable for casting.

questions.text: Describe one important use of bleaching powder in water treatment. Write the relevant chemical reaction.

key_points: Bleaching powder releases Cl2 / HClO when dissolved in water
Ca(OCl)Cl + H2O → Ca(OH)2 + Cl2; or Ca(OCl)Cl + CO2 + H2O → CaCO3 + HClO + HCl
HClO / Cl2 kills pathogens → disinfects drinking water / swimming pools
rubric.expected_answer: Bleaching powder is used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pools. When dissolved in water it releases nascent chlorine/hypochlorous acid (HClO) which kills pathogens. Reaction: Ca(OCl)Cl + CO2 + H2O produces CaCO3 + HClO + HCl; the HClO acts as the disinfecting agent.

questions.text: 20 mL of NaOH solution is exactly neutralised by 16 mL of H2SO4 solution. What volume of the same H2SO4 solution will neutralise 30 mL of the same NaOH solution?

rubric.expected_answer: 24 mL
